Lena Marsh found the knight on a Tuesday afternoon at Corliss Park, after her little brother had spent most of an hour digging in the sandbox for what he said was a dinosaur. What he brought up instead was a white chess piece, carved from wood and about as tall as her thumb, with a chip out of one ear and a circle of green felt glued to its base. The wood of the horse's mane had gone pale and smooth, as if someone had pushed the piece forward by that spot a great many times.

She carried it home in her jacket pocket and stood it on the windowsill above the sink. Her father picked it up while he was drying dishes and turned it over under the light. "Somebody made this," he said. "See the knife marks under the chin? Nobody sells pieces like this at a toy store."

The next morning she asked at the park office, where a woman behind the counter brought out a cardboard box of lost things: mittens, a retainer case, a single roller skate, a library book two years overdue. There was nothing in it that belonged with a chess knight.

The sandbox was twenty steps from the four stone tables along the east path, where on Saturday mornings a few old men played chess with sets they brought from home. On weekdays the tables held only pigeons.

So on Saturday she walked to the tables with the knight in her fist. One game was going. Two men sat across from each other under a gray umbrella, and among the white pieces, in the middle of the board, stood the cap from a bottle of ginger ale, upside down. As Lena watched, the man playing white picked up the cap and moved it two squares forward and one to the side.

She set the knight on the edge of the table. The man gave it a long, level look. He did not smile or start or reach for it quickly. He turned it once to find the chipped ear, put the bottle cap in his shirt pocket, and stood the knight on the square the cap had left. Only then did he look up at her.

"Three weeks," said the other man, who introduced himself as Mr. Dahl. "Three weeks he has been playing with a bottle cap, and he says it was the cap that cost him two games."

The man with the knight was Mr. Ruiz. His grandson, he explained, had carried the set to the sandbox one afternoon to show the other children, and when Mr. Ruiz counted the pieces that evening he came up one short. He had gone back the next day and raked through the sand with his fingers until the light went.

Then he returned to the game. He moved the knight, and after a minute, still looking at the board, he said that Lena could play black next Saturday if she knew how the horse moved. She did, as it happened. She had been watching the bottle cap.

For ninety years it stood above the choir loft,
eleven hundred pipes, the tallest
as wide around as a stovepipe, the smallest
no thicker than a pencil, and one low F
that sounded by itself on rainy Sundays.

Mrs. Okonkwo taught me on it Tuesdays
after school. My feet were too short at first
to reach the pedals, so I played them standing,
holding the bench, while the whole building
hummed in the soles of my shoes like a ship.

On Saturday the men came with a truck
and a dealer's list, and by evening
the pipes lay in the parking lot in rows,
like oars, each one numbered in chalk,
while the church council stood around with coffee.

On Sunday a cabinet stood in their place,
walnut-colored, with two speakers and a cord,
and a card on the music stand: Sixty
authentic pipe-organ voices at the touch
of a button. Never needs tuning.

Never needs tuning. As if the tuning
were the trouble. As if a thing that had come through
the flood of 1937 and four pastors
could be traded for a cabinet in a weekend
by people who had sat beneath it all their lives
and looked up only at the hymn board.

I will not call this grief. Grief belongs
to weather and to accidents. Somebody
read the dealer's offer, and somebody
chose a Saturday, so the ones who played it
would hear about it last.

Tomorrow at six I will climb to the loft
and play the cabinet with every stop pulled out,
the same three hymns, each note
exactly where it ought to be, and every note wrong.

eleven hundred pipes, the tallest
as wide around as a stovepipe, the smallest
no thicker than a pencil, and one low F

hummed in the soles of my shoes like a ship.

On Saturday the men came with a truck
and a dealer's list, and by evening
the pipes lay in the parking lot in rows,
like oars, each one numbered in chalk,
while the church council stood around with coffee.

On Sunday a cabinet stood in their place,
walnut-colored, with two speakers and a cord,
and a card on the music stand: Sixty
authentic pipe-organ voices at the touch
of a button. Never needs tuning.

were the trouble. As if a thing that had come through
the flood of 1937 and four pastors
could be traded for a cabinet in a weekend
by people who had sat beneath it all their lives
and looked up only at the hymn board.

I will not call this grief. Grief belongs
to weather and to accidents. Somebody
read the dealer's offer, and somebody
chose a Saturday, so the ones who played it
would hear about it last.

and play the cabinet with every stop pulled out,
the same three hymns, each note
exactly where it ought to be, and every note wrong.

The winter I was thirteen, I fenced épée in a long room above Dunn's Hardware, where two strips of blue tape ran the length of the floor and the radiators knocked all evening like someone asking to be let in. Our coach was a small, gray-haired woman named Ines Varga, who had fenced in college and who carried a pencil behind one ear for reasons that became clear in the first week.

For six weeks she let none of us hold a blade. We advanced and retreated along the tape, lunged at the empty air, and recovered, again and again, while she walked beside us and tapped the back of a knee with her pencil whenever it bent the wrong way. I had joined to stab people, more or less, and I spent those weeks counting radiator knocks.

Épée is the easiest of the three weapons to explain. For six springs I have paid part of my rent by painting names on the backs of boats at a yard on the Callow River. The work is simple to describe: a stencil, a fine brush, a steady wrist, and gold leaf if the owner is paying for it. The names are harder to describe, and I have come to think they are the most honest writing I will ever be paid to copy.

Puns are the most common, by a wide margin: Knot Working, Reel Time, Sea Note, and something called Aqua Holic that I have lettered on three different hulls. Next come the names of wives, husbands, and daughters, then wishes (Second Wind, Fair Enough, Lucky Break), and finally a small, steady supply of warnings. In six years I have painted eleven boats called some version of Serenity, and one called Bad Idea.

Part of the reason, I think, is that a boat name is chosen differently from most names. A car gets its plate from the state, a string of letters and numbers nobody has to defend. A child is named before anyone knows who the child will be. A boat owner chooses a name for a thing already bought and paid for, and then has it painted in letters a foot high where everyone on the dock will read it.

Many sailors hold that renaming a boat brings bad luck unless the old name is first removed from everything that carries it, the logbook and the life ring as well as the stern, and the sea is formally told of the change. I have scraped off more old names than I have painted new ones. Owners who laugh at the custom are the ones most likely to ask, when the scraping is done, whether I got all of it.

One man had me paint Just This Once on a small blue sloop and explained, without being asked, that his wife had agreed to a single summer. The next April he came back to the yard, stood beside me while I scraped, and asked for Just Once More.

I used to roll my eyes at the puns. These days I laugh at Knot Working every time a new one comes in, which is most years, and when the owner of Bad Idea asked for six-inch letters I gave him ten, because the name seemed to deserve them. We tend to say a name is a label, a way of telling one thing from another. On the river it is closer to a sentence the owner has agreed to stand behind, in public, in gold.

For half a century, the standard test of whether an animal can recognize itself has been simple to describe. Researchers place a colored mark on part of an animal's body that it can see only in a mirror, then watch what it does when it is given one. A chimpanzee that touches the mark on its own face, rather than reaching for the image, is taken to understand that the reflection is itself. Chimpanzees passed in 1970. Most species tested since then have failed.

In 2019 a team led by the biologist Masanori Kohda at Osaka City University reported that a small reef fish had passed. The fish was the bluestreak cleaner wrasse, which makes its living by picking parasites and dead skin off the bodies of larger fish, and the team's study proceeded in steps.

First, the researchers put a mirror in each fish's tank. For the first few days most of the fish treated their reflections as rivals, opening their mouths and charging at the glass. Then the attacks faded, and the fish began doing things they were seldom seen doing otherwise, such as swimming upside down in front of the mirror or darting toward it and stopping short.

Next, the team injected a small brown mark under the skin of each fish's throat, a spot the fish could see only in the mirror. Most of the marked fish, after looking at their reflections, scraped their throats against the sand or a rock on the bottom of the tank, a behavior wrasses use to rid their skin of irritations. Two comparisons gave the result its weight: fish given a clear, colorless injection in the same place seldom scraped, and fish with brown marks seldom scraped when no mirror was present.

Not everyone accepted the conclusion. Critics, among them the psychologist who first ran the mirror test on chimpanzees, pointed out that a brown spot on a cleaner wrasse looks very much like the parasites the fish spends its life removing from others. A fish built to notice such spots, they argued, might scrape at one without understanding who was in the mirror. The researchers answered that the fish scraped only after seeing the mark in the reflection, which is exactly what the test asks for.

The disagreement has turned out to be about the test as much as about the fish. Either a fish can recognize itself, or the mark test can be passed by an animal that does not, and the test has been the main evidence for every species on the short list since 1970.

For half a century, the standard test of whether an animal can recognize itself has been simple to describe. Researchers place a colored mark on part of an animal's body that it can see only in a mirror, then watch what it does when it is given one. A chimpanzee that touches the mark on its own face, rather than reaching for the image, is taken to understand that the reflection is itself. Chimpanzees passed in 1970. Most species tested since then have failed.

In 2019 a team led by the biologist Masanori Kohda at Osaka City University reported that a small reef fish had passed. The fish was the bluestreak cleaner wrasse, which makes its living by picking parasites and dead skin off the bodies of larger fish, and the team's study proceeded in steps.

First, the researchers put a mirror in each fish's tank. For the first few days most of the fish treated their reflections as rivals, opening their mouths and charging at the glass. Then the attacks faded, and the fish began doing things they were seldom seen doing otherwise, such as swimming upside down in front of the mirror or darting toward it and stopping short.

Next, the team injected a small brown mark under the skin of each fish's throat, a spot the fish could see only in the mirror. Most of the marked fish, after looking at their reflections, scraped their throats against the sand or a rock on the bottom of the tank, a behavior wrasses use to rid their skin of irritations. Two comparisons gave the result its weight: fish given a clear, colorless injection in the same place seldom scraped, and fish with brown marks seldom scraped when no mirror was present.

Not everyone accepted the conclusion. Critics, among them the psychologist who first ran the mirror test on chimpanzees, pointed out that a brown spot on a cleaner wrasse looks very much like the parasites the fish spends its life removing from others. A fish built to notice such spots, they argued, might scrape at one without understanding who was in the mirror. The researchers answered that the fish scraped only after seeing the mark in the reflection, which is exactly what the test asks for.

The disagreement has turned out to be about the test as much as about the fish. Either a fish can recognize itself, or the mark test can be passed by an animal that does not, and the test has been the main evidence for every species on the short list since 1970.
